Changing management

How to leave your property management company in DC

For Washington, DC condo boards · Updated November 14, 2026

The short answer

Start with your management contract: it sets the notice period, any termination fee, and what the company must hand back. If the developer signed the contract while it still controlled the association, DC law lets the association end it without penalty on at least 90 days' written notice (§ 42-1903.02). Plan for about 90 days: vote, give notice, move the bank accounts, collect the records, and tell owners where to pay.

1. Read the management contract

The contract decides most of what follows. Find:

  • The term and renewal date, and whether it renews automatically.
  • Whether the board can end it for any reason or only for cause.
  • The notice period, and how notice must be delivered.
  • Any termination fee.
  • What the company must return at the end, and how quickly.
  • Who controls the bank accounts and any software that holds the association's data.

2. Contracts the developer signed

If the declarant (the developer) signed the management contract on the association's behalf while it still controlled the board, the DC Condominium Act lets the association end it without penalty on at least 90 days' written notice (§ 42-1903.02).

3. Vote, then give notice

Vote to end the contract at a properly noticed board meeting and record the vote in the minutes. Send written notice exactly as the contract requires; certified mail with a return receipt gives you proof of the date.

4. Get the association's records back

The records belong to the association, which must keep detailed records of its receipts and expenditures and make its books available to owners (§ 42-1903.14). Ask for:

AreaWhat to collect
MoneyBank statements and online access for the operating and reserve accounts, the general ledger, the current year's budget, prior year financial statements, tax returns and any audit.
OwnersEvery owner's ledger and balance, delinquency and collection files, payment plans, autopay details, and the owner contact list.
ContractsVendor and service contracts, insurance policies and certificates, and warranties.
GovernanceThe declaration, bylaws, rules, minutes, resolutions and election records.
BuildingThe reserve study, maintenance and inspection records, permits, keys, fobs and access codes.

5. A 90 day timeline

WhenWhat happens
Day 0Board vote. Written notice sent. Ask for the records list in writing.
By day 30Open or confirm bank accounts in the association's name and update the signers. Set up how owners will pay.
By day 60Tell vendors and the insurance agent who to contact and where invoices go. Load owners, balances and documents into your new system.
Day 90Switch day. Confirm every record has arrived and balances match the last statement.
First month afterClose the first month yourselves and send every owner a statement.

6. Tell the owners

Send every owner one notice with the switch date, new payment instructions, how to set up autopay, and who to call. Send it early and again a week before switch day.
